description: OS functions, utility programs, and audit trails and code reviews for robust software.
content_html:
What Is an Operating System?

Every computer needs a layer of software that manages its hardware resources and provides a platform on which applications can run. This is the operating system (OS). Without an OS, every application would need to contain its own code to communicate with hardware — an impossible duplication of effort. Instead, applications request services from the OS, and the OS handles the low-level work.

Your exam requires you to know four specific functions of an operating system: file management, process management, peripheral management and user management. Each addresses a different aspect of running a computer system reliably.

Key Fact

The four OS functions you must know: File management (organising, storing and retrieving files), Process management (deciding which programs get CPU time and when), Peripheral management (handling communication with input/output devices), User management (creating accounts, setting permissions and controlling access).

The Four OS Functions in Detail

File management keeps track of where every file is stored on secondary storage. The OS maintains a directory structure (folders within folders), tracks file names, sizes and locations, and enforces access permissions (who is allowed to read or modify a file). When you save a document, the OS decides where on the storage device to place it and updates its records.

Process management handles multiple programs running at the same time. A modern computer might have dozens of processes active — the browser, the music player, the background virus scan. The OS switches the CPU between them so quickly that they all appear to run simultaneously. It also manages what happens when a process needs to wait (e.g. for a file to load) — pausing that process and giving the CPU to something else.

Peripheral management allows the CPU to communicate with hardware devices such as printers, keyboards, screens and storage devices. Because each device is different, the OS uses a device driver — a small program that translates between the OS’s standard instructions and the specific commands a particular device understands. When you plug in a new printer, the OS loads or downloads the appropriate driver.

User management allows different people to use the same computer with separate settings and access rights. A school network, for example, might allow students to save files only in their own folder and block access to system settings, while giving network administrators full control. Each user has an account with a defined set of permissions.

Utility Software

Utility software carries out maintenance tasks. Unlike application software (which helps users complete their own work), utility programs serve the system itself. The five utility types on your specification are file repair, backup, data compression, disk defragmentation and anti-malware.

File repair — attempts to recover files that have become corrupted or unreadable. This can happen if a drive develops bad sectors, a file is partially overwritten, or a program crashes mid-save. A file repair utility scans for corruption and rebuilds as much of the file as possible.

Backup utility — creates copies of files and stores them in a secondary location (another drive, a network server, or an external device). If the original files are lost or corrupted, they can be restored from the backup. Backup utilities can be scheduled to run automatically so that copies are kept up to date.

Data compression utility — reduces the size of files so they take up less storage space or can be transferred more quickly. Some compression is lossless (the original can be perfectly reconstructed); other compression is lossy (some quality is permanently discarded). A file archiver (such as a ZIP tool) is a common example of lossless compression utility software.

Disk defragmentation — reorganises files on a magnetic hard disk. Over time, as files are added, deleted and modified, their data becomes fragmented — scattered in non-contiguous sections across the disk surface. A defragmenter moves fragments together so the read/write head needs to travel less, speeding up file access. Note: SSDs do not benefit from defragmentation (and it can reduce their lifespan), so this utility applies to magnetic HDDs only.

Anti-malware — detects, quarantines and removes malicious software (malware) such as viruses, spyware and ransomware. It does this by scanning files against a database of known malware signatures, or by monitoring for suspicious behaviour. Anti-malware is a utility because it maintains the health and security of the system rather than performing a user task.

Robust Software: Why It Matters

Robust software is software that continues to work correctly even when things do not go as planned — unexpected inputs, high traffic, or deliberate attempts to exploit a weakness. In safety-critical systems (medical devices, banking, aircraft control), a software failure can have serious real-world consequences. Even in everyday applications, a crash or a vulnerability that leaks user data is costly.

Developing robust software requires identifying vulnerabilities before they can be exploited. Two methods the specification requires you to know are audit trails and code reviews.

A code review is a design-time technique. Before the software is released, one or more developers read through the source code written by a colleague, looking for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses and poor practices. A fresh pair of eyes often catches vulnerabilities the original developer missed. Code reviews are particularly effective at identifying issues such as missing input validation (which could allow malicious data to crash the program) or hardcoded passwords.

An audit trail is a run-time technique. While the software is in use, it automatically records a timestamped log of significant actions: which user logged in, which files were accessed, what data was changed and when. If a security incident occurs — say, a database record is altered without authorisation — the audit trail provides a record of what happened, when, and under which account. This makes it possible to trace breaches and investigate suspicious activity.

The key distinction: a code review happens before the software runs (during development) and aims to prevent vulnerabilities from shipping. An audit trail happens while the software runs (at runtime) and aims to detect and trace problems after they occur.

Key Fact

A code review is a design-time technique: developers read each other’s source code before release to find bugs and security weaknesses. An audit trail is a run-time technique: the system automatically logs who did what and when, so security breaches can be traced. Code reviews prevent problems; audit trails detect and record them.
exam_tip_html: When describing OS functions, use precise language — ‘file management’ is not the same as ‘managing the CPU’. Exam questions often give a scenario and ask you to ‘Explain’ which OS function is involved: match the scenario to exactly one of the four functions. For robust software, the key distinction examiners test is design-time vs run-time: code review happens before the software is released; an audit trail runs while the software is live. Always include both the what and the why — don’t just name audit trail, say “it logs user actions so that security breaches can be detected and traced.”
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • An operating system manages four areas: file management (organising files), process management (allocating CPU time), peripheral management (communicating with devices via drivers) and user management (accounts and permissions).
  • Utility software maintains the system: file repair, backup, data compression, disk defragmentation (HDDs only) and anti-malware are the five types required by the specification.
  • Robust software resists failure and exploits. Code reviews (design-time: developers inspect code before release) and audit trails (run-time: automatic logs of who did what and when) are two methods for identifying and tracking vulnerabilities.

practice_questions.text: Name two functions of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any two of the four: file management / process management / peripheral management / user management.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by process management as a function of an operating system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: the OS controls which programs are running at any time (1 mark) and allocates CPU time between them, switching between processes so they appear to run simultaneously (1 mark). Accept references to pausing waiting processes or scheduling.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a code review helps developers create more robust software.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review involves one or more developers reading through code written by a colleague before it is released. The reviewer looks for bugs, logic errors, security weaknesses (e.g. missing input validation, hardcoded credentials) and poor coding practices. Because the reviewer did not write the code, they approach it with fresh eyes and can spot issues the original developer overlooked. Identifying vulnerabilities at design time means they can be fixed before users are exposed to them, making the software safer and more reliable.
Secure: States that code review involves another developer checking the code for errors or vulnerabilities before release, with some explanation of why a second perspective is valuable.
Developing: States that a code review involves checking code for errors, without explaining the mechanism or benefit.
Emerging: Vague reference to checking code.

practice_questions.text: Describe the purpose of an audit trail in a software system.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks for: an audit trail is an automatic log (1 mark) that records who performed each action, what was changed, and when, so that security incidents or unauthorised access can be traced or detected (1 mark).

practice_questions.text: Explain one difference between a code review and an audit trail as methods of making software more robust.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A code review is a design-time technique carried out before the software is released: developers inspect source code to find and fix vulnerabilities before users encounter them. An audit trail is a run-time technique that operates while the software is live: it logs actions automatically so that if something goes wrong (e.g. a data breach), there is a record of what happened and when. The key difference is timing and purpose: code review prevents problems from shipping; audit trails detect and allow investigation of problems after they occur.
Secure: Identifies that one is before release and one operates during use, with some explanation of each.
Developing: Names both techniques and states one difference without development.
Emerging: Names both techniques with no difference stated.

practice_questions.text: Identify which utility program a system administrator would use if files on a magnetic hard disk were taking much longer to open than usual, and explain why this utility would help.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Disk defragmentation. Over time, files on a magnetic HDD become fragmented — their data is split across non-contiguous sectors of the platter. When a file is opened, the read/write head must physically move to each fragment in turn, increasing access time. Defragmentation reorganises the file data so it is stored in contiguous sectors, meaning the head travels less distance and access is faster. Notes that defragmentation applies to HDDs, not SSDs.
Secure: Identifies defragmentation and explains that fragmented files cause the head to move more, slowing access.
Developing: Identifies defragmentation without a full explanation of why fragmentation causes slowness.
Emerging: Names a utility but incorrect or no explanation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which OS function is responsible for allocating CPU time to multiple programs so they appear to run simultaneously?
A code review is best described as which type of technique for improving software robustness?
options: Run-time — it runs while the software is live
Design-time — it happens before the software is released
Post-deployment — it analyses logs after a breach
Automated — it runs without any developer involvement

knowledge_checks.q: An audit trail records who performed each action and _____, so security incidents can be traced.
Disk defragmentation improves file access speed on magnetic hard disks by reorganising fragmented files into _____ sectors.
Match each OS function to what it manages:
right: Accounts, permissions and access rights for different users
Organising, storing and retrieving files on storage devices
Allocating CPU time between running programs

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four functions of an operating system required by the specification.
flashcard_questions.a: File management, process management, peripheral management, user management.

flashcard_questions.q: What does peripheral management allow the OS to do?
flashcard_questions.a: Communicate with input/output devices using device drivers.
A small program that translates OS instructions into commands a specific device understands.
Software that performs maintenance tasks to keep the system running efficiently.

flashcard_questions.q: Which utility program reorganises fragmented files on a magnetic hard disk?
Why does defragmentation not benefit SSDs?
flashcard_questions.a: SSDs have no moving parts, so there is no mechanical penalty for non-contiguous data.
A design-time check where developers read each other's code to find bugs and vulnerabilities before release.
A run-time log that records who performed each action and when, to detect or trace security incidents.

flashcard_questions.q: Is a code review a design-time or run-time technique?
flashcard_questions.a: Design-time — it happens before the software is released.

flashcard_questions.q: Is an audit trail a design-time or run-time technique?
flashcard_questions.a: Run-time — it logs actions while the software is being used.
Software that operates reliably under a wide range of conditions, including unexpected inputs and attempted exploits.

glossary_terms.definition: A type of system software that manages hardware resources and provides services for application software, handling file, process, peripheral and user management.
An OS function that organises files into a directory structure, controls access permissions, and manages reading and writing to storage.
An OS function that manages which programs are running, allocates CPU time between them, and switches between processes so the computer appears to run multiple programs simultaneously.
An OS function that manages communication between the computer and its input and output devices, using device drivers to translate between the OS and specific hardware.
An OS function that creates and manages user accounts, sets access permissions, and controls what each user is allowed to do on the system.
Software that performs maintenance or support tasks for the computer system rather than directly serving the end user's primary work.
Software that operates reliably and correctly under a wide range of conditions, including unexpected inputs, high load and attempts to exploit vulnerabilities.
A chronological log of events automatically recorded by a system, capturing who performed each action, what was changed, and when — used to detect and investigate security incidents.
A design-time technique in which developers read through each other's source code before release to find bugs, logic errors and security weaknesses.
